strengths: Introduces ConceptDrift, a novel weight-space approach for bias identification that analyzes the drift of a linear probe initialized with class-name embeddings, moving beyond data-only or misclassified-sample-based protocols.

The method is intuitive, flexible, and applicable to multiple modalities, demonstrated on image datasets (Waterbirds, CelebA, NICO++) and a text dataset (CivilComments) using foundation models such as CLIP and mGTE.
Reports consistent improvements in worst-group zero-shot accuracy over baselines including B2T, SpLiCE, and Lg on several datasets, with an ablation study on ranking score and number of concepts.
Provides qualitative bias examples, an appendix with a cosine-similarity bound, and a discussion of limitations and broader impacts.
Paper is generally well written and well organized, with clear figures and a coherent motivation.
weaknesses: The main evaluation of bias quality is potentially circular and unfair: discovered biases are inserted into zero-shot prompts and the best prompt is selected via max over templates. It is not clear whether this selection uses validation or test data; if test data is used, it constitutes test-time tuning and invalidates the comparison. The baseline uses a single prompt while bias-based methods use many candidate prompts, giving an unfair advantage.

Average accuracy often drops substantially (e.g., CivilComments from 83.4 to 69.0), which contradicts the broad claim of significantly improving zero-shot performance. The paper does not adequately discuss this trade-off.

Baseline comparisons are incomplete: not all methods are evaluated on all datasets, and there are no controls for random concepts or matched prompt counts. Standard spurious-correlation discovery methods are not compared.

The number of selected concepts (top-q) is arbitrary, with the authors leaving a principled cut-off strategy for future work. This undermines fully automatic bias identification and raises concerns about hyperparameter tuning on test data.

The theoretical support is limited: the cosine-similarity bound only provides a lower bound under strong assumptions, while the ranking score in Eq. 3 remains a heuristic and is not analyzed for robustness.

Qualitative bias extraction lacks quantitative human validation. Many extracted concepts may be noisy, class-related, or artifacts of the captioning/keyword extraction pipeline rather than genuine spurious correlations.
Reproducibility is limited: no code release is mentioned, and important details such as dataset splits, random seeds, and the validation/test protocol for prompt selection are not fully specified.

The novelty is moderate: analyzing linear probe weights and embedding-space concept scores is related to existing interpretability and concept-based methods, and the practical gain over prior bias-discovery approaches is not sufficiently isolated.
